title: CogniDir: Combating Cognitive Malicious Comments via Adaptive Distributional Learning for Robust Fake News Detection
cardSummary: Adaptive training against LLM-generated malicious comments for robust fake news detection.
tldr: CogniDir strengthens comment-aware fake news detection through mechanism-specific malicious comment generation and feedback-driven training mixtures. InfoDirichlet Resampling adapts exposure across attack groups on Weibo16, Weibo20, and RumourEval-19.
abstract: CogniDir reformulates robust fake news detection as adaptive distributional learning. It builds mechanism-specific adversarial comments covering fact distortion, logical confusion, and emotional manipulation, then maps group-wise vulnerability to sampling proportions through a Dirichlet-mean parameterization. The resulting allocation smoothly shifts training exposure toward the most brittle attack mechanisms. Across Weibo16, Weibo20, and RumourEval-19, CogniDir improves F1 by up to 17.9% and reduces mean attack success rate by 45%.

methodOverview: CogniDir works in three stages: mechanism-specific malicious comment generation, InfoDirichlet Resampling that updates the training mixture from group vulnerability after each epoch, and robust evaluation under mixed adversarial comments. The mixture uses the Dirichlet mean, a smooth closed-form allocation that tracks the weakest attack group.
contributions: A cognitive-grounded synthesis pipeline that produces mechanism-labeled comments for fact distortion, logical confusion, and emotional manipulation.
InfoDirichlet Resampling, which turns group-wise vulnerability into an adaptive training mixture through the Dirichlet mean.
Strong robustness on Weibo16, Weibo20, and RumourEval-19, with up to +17.9% F1 and a 45% reduction in mean ASR.
mainResults: On Weibo16, CogniDir keeps F1 near 0.94 across attack categories, while prior detectors drop sharply under diverse malicious comments.
Robust F1 improves by +9.0% on Weibo16, +17.9% on Weibo20 (Macro-F1 0.947), and +14.5% on RumourEval-19 over the strongest baselines.
Adaptive training reduces mean ASR by 45%, down to 0.116, across attack types and comment counts.
Malicious-comment generation, vulnerability scoring, and Dirichlet expectation allocation each contribute to the final robustness.
priorWorkDiff: CogniDir assigns training exposure to distinct attack mechanisms and updates the mixture from group-wise vulnerability feedback. InfoDirichlet Resampling maps the scores to positive Dirichlet parameters and uses the normalized mean as the next training mixture.

attackCategories.name: Fact Distortion
attackCategories.description: Injects unverified or misleading factual details to create false credibility and encourage dissemination.

attackCategories.name: Logical Confusion
attackCategories.description: Exploits causal fallacies and contradictory reasoning to undermine the detector's verification boundaries.

attackCategories.name: Emotional Manipulation
attackCategories.description: Uses affective framing and social pressure to shift attention away from veracity signals in the news–comment pair.

faqs.q: How do social comments affect fake news detection?
faqs.a: Comment-aware detectors use social responses together with news content. Manipulated comments can alter this evidence and affect the detector's predictions. CogniDir evaluates this behavior under LLM-generated cognitive malicious comments.

faqs.q: Which cognitive attack mechanisms are studied?
faqs.a: The study evaluates fact distortion, logical confusion, and emotional manipulation as separate comment attack groups. Group-wise results characterize detector vulnerability across these mechanisms.

faqs.q: How does CogniDir adapt adversarial training?
faqs.a: After each epoch, the framework scores attack-group vulnerability using accuracy and probabilistic confidence. InfoDirichlet Resampling converts these scores into Dirichlet parameters and uses the Dirichlet mean to set the next training mixture.

faqs.q: How does group-wise evaluation guide training exposure?
faqs.a: Group-wise measurements track how the detector responds to each attack mechanism. The allocation gives vulnerable groups additional exposure and updates the mixture as the detector learns.

faqs.q: Which datasets and languages are evaluated?
faqs.a: The experiments use Weibo16, Weibo20, and RumourEval-19, covering Chinese and English comment-based fake news detection. The evaluation reports detection performance across attack mechanisms and comment settings.

faqs.q: Which components are available in the repository?
faqs.a: The repository provides training and evaluation entry points, model and sampling modules, and data-format documentation. The project resources link to the training script, evaluation script, and setup instructions.

researchQuestion: How can fake news detectors adapt to different mechanisms of LLM-generated malicious comments?
researchContext: Comment-aware fake news detectors combine news content with social responses. LLM-generated malicious comments can manipulate this context through fact distortion, logical confusion, and emotional manipulation. CogniDir studies these mechanisms as distinct sources of detector vulnerability.

The framework connects adversarial social-context evaluation with adaptive training-data allocation. It scores vulnerability across attack groups and uses a Dirichlet-mean allocation to update training exposure. Experiments on Weibo16, Weibo20, and RumourEval-19 evaluate robustness across attack mechanisms and comment settings.

researchNote.title: Robust Fake News Detection under Adversarial Social Context
researchNote.description: A research overview of malicious comment attacks, cognitive manipulation, and adaptive training mixtures for robust fake news detection.
researchNote.author: Chunlin Gong
researchNote.lead: Social responses are an important input for comment-aware fake news detection. They also create an attack surface: malicious comments can manipulate the context used by a detector. Research on this problem connects adversarial text generation, mechanism-specific evaluation, and adaptive robust training.

sections.title: Studying adversarial social context
paragraphs: A social-context evaluation records the news item, the comments supplied to the detector, and the resulting prediction. LLMs make it possible to generate comments with different rhetorical and cognitive mechanisms, creating structured tests of detector robustness.

CogniDir studies fact distortion, logical confusion, and emotional manipulation as distinct attack groups. This organization connects the design of malicious comments with group-wise vulnerability measurements.

sections.title: Measuring vulnerability across mechanisms
paragraphs: Aggregate detection performance summarizes the overall result, while group-wise measurements reveal how the detector responds to different attacks. Evaluating several comment settings makes this view useful for studying the effect of both attack mechanism and context composition.

The CogniDir experiments use Weibo16, Weibo20, and RumourEval-19. The project page presents detection results, attack success rates, and ablations of malicious comment generation, vulnerability scoring, and allocation.

sections.title: Adapting the training mixture
paragraphs: Adaptive training allocates exposure according to the detector's current vulnerabilities. In CogniDir, group-wise accuracy and probabilistic confidence inform vulnerability scores. InfoDirichlet Resampling maps these scores to Dirichlet parameters and uses the mean to set the next training mixture.
This feedback connects evaluation with training: the detector is assessed across attack mechanisms, the allocation is updated, and subsequent training responds to the measured weaknesses.

sections.title: Connecting generation, sampling, and defense
paragraphs: Generate First, Then Sample studies LLM-generated fake news and reinforcement-learning-based sampling of real and fake training examples. SINCon studies malicious message injection in rumor detection and uses contrastive learning to make node influence more uniform in message propagation trees.

CogniDir contributes mechanism-specific malicious comments and feedback-driven allocation across attack groups. These methods provide useful reference points for researchers studying generated training data, adversarial social context, and adaptive robustness. The linked project page and repository collect the experiments, training entry points, and official EMNLP 2026 citation.
